subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

section_titles: Representing 3-digit numbers with tiles and number line
periods.activity_title: Tiles and Lines: Picturing Three-Digit Numbers

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q (draw tiles), p.118
tasks_in_class.description: Draw tiles like the driver to show 832, 947, 726, 504, 620, 700 in your notebook.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q (number line 1), p.118
tasks_in_class.description: Locate 530, 540, 628, 696, 590 on the number line (500–700).

homework.book_ref: Let us Do Q (number line 2), p.118

time_bands.activity: Introduce the tile model: hold up or sketch a flat (100), long (10), and unit (1) tile on the board. Ask children how many of each type a number like 243 needs. Elicit the H-T-O link through class discussion.
Students work on Let us Do Q (draw tiles), p.118 ("Draw tiles like the driver to show 832, 947, 726….") in notebooks. Circulate and prompt: 'How many flats do you need for the hundreds digit?'

Introduce the partial number line (500–700) on the board, marking equal intervals together. Students then complete Let us Do Q (number line 1), p.118 ("Locate 530, 540, 628, 696, 590…."), placing each number independently.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is drawing one tile per digit rather than one tile per unit — a child may draw three unit tiles for 3 hundreds instead of three flat tiles. Prompt: 'A flat stands for a whole hundred; how many ones would you need to replace it?' The number-line task builds on the tile groupings by asking students to reason about equal intervals rather than count every tick mark.

section_titles: Estimating position: neighbouring hundreds, fifties, and tens
periods.activity_title: Neighbours and Crane Jumps: Placing Numbers in Intervals

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think Q1, p.119
tasks_in_class.description: Write neighbouring hundreds, fifties, and tens for 183, 345, 693, 734, 899.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think Q2 (crane 1), p.119
tasks_in_class.description: Help the crane: find steps and step length for 667−__=650 and 667+__=700.

homework.description: Help the crane: find steps and step length for __−__=750 and __+__=800.

time_bands.activity: Draw a number line segment on the board and place 468, asking: 'Which hundred is just below 468? Which is just above?' Model the worked example from the book before asking students to try their own.

Pairs work on Let us Think Q1, p.119 ("Write neighbouring hundreds, fifties, and tens for 183, 345, 693, 734, 899."). Share answers class-wide; discuss why the neighbouring fifty of 693 is 650 and 700.

Introduce the crane picture and explain the backward-jump (worm) and forward-jump (fish) idea. Students solve Let us Think Q2 (crane 1), p.119 ("find steps and step length for 667−__=650 and 667+__=700") and discuss what step length the crane used.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse the 'neighbouring fifty' with simply the nearest round number; reinforce that neighbouring fifties are multiples of 50. The crane activity builds on the neighbouring-interval thinking by casting the same idea as a physical jump, making the distance between a number and its neighbour tangible.

section_titles: Tambola: number properties and multiple representations
periods.activity_title: Footprints and Tambola: Skipping and Knowing Numbers

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Skip and Solve (footprint trails), p.121
tasks_in_class.description: Complete the skip-count footprint trails: consecutive sequences 940–969 with missing numbers.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Skip and Solve (branching diagram), p.121
tasks_in_class.description: Fill missing boxes in the branching skip pattern: +10, +100, +25, +30, +15 from starting values.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think Q3 (Tambola), p.120
tasks_in_class.description: Fill a 4×4 grid with numbers 570–630; cross out numbers matching 6 given clues.

time_bands.activity: Write a short skip sequence on the board (e.g., 500, 510, 520, __, __) and invite students to call out the missing values, naming the step size aloud.

Students work on Skip and Solve (footprint trails), p.121 ("Complete the skip-count footprint trails: 940–969….") followed by Skip and Solve (branching diagram), p.121 ("Fill missing boxes: +10, +100, +25, +30, +15…."). Pause after the footprint trails to confirm step sizes before the branching diagram.

Introduce Tambola: each student writes any 16 numbers from 570–630 in a 4×4 grid. Read the six clues one at a time; students cross out matching entries. Discuss how each clue type (digit property, range, relative value) uses place-value knowledge to identify numbers.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent skip-count error is applying the wrong step when the branching diagram changes direction — remind students to re-read the step label on each branch. The Tambola game applies the same place-value fluency built in the skip activity in a game setting, reinforcing that clues like 'tens digit is 9' require inspecting individual digit positions.
materials: Blank 4×4 grid drawn on paper or board for Tambola

section_titles: Tambola: number properties and multiple representations
periods.activity_title: Many Ways to Say a Number, Many Ways to Order

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think Q (multiple representations), p.120
tasks_in_class.description: Write different ways of making 368, 555, 905, 736 (e.g., 3 hundreds 6 tens 8 ones, 300+60+8, 400−32).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q1 (number sentences), p.122
tasks_in_class.description: Write number sentences for the centre numbers 400 (e.g., 290+110) and 775 (e.g., 750+25).

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q3 (circle puzzle), p.122
tasks_in_class.description: Fill 384, 23, 176, 905 in empty circles so ordering conditions are met.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q4 (match quantities), p.123
tasks_in_class.description: Match real-world quantities (children in school, books in classroom, etc.) to number ranges 0–10 through more than 1000.

homework.description: Write numbers in blank spaces satisfying greater-than/less-than conditions around 400, with anchors 419, 425, 385, 436.

time_bands.activity: Students work on Let us Think Q (multiple representations), p.120 ("Write different ways of making 368, 555, 905, 736…."). Share two or three contrasting representations for 368 on the board to show that addition and subtraction forms are both valid.
Students attempt Let us Do Q1 (number sentences), p.122 ("Write number sentences for 400 and 775….") in pairs, competing to find the most representations. Collect diverse responses on the board.

Students complete Let us Do Q3 (circle puzzle), p.122 ("Fill 384, 23, 176, 905 in circles so ordering conditions are met.") and Let us Do Q4 (match quantities), p.123 ("Match real-world quantities to number ranges…."). Discuss the match task as a class to address estimation reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error in the multiple-representations task is writing only the expanded form (300+60+8) and missing subtraction forms; prompt students to think of a near-hundred and subtract. The circle-puzzle ordering task is accessible after the representations work because students have been reasoning about a number's value from multiple angles.

section_titles: The Number Detective: special number patterns
periods.activity_title: Riddles and Detectives: Clues, Descriptions, and Number Families

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q5 (riddle match), p.123
tasks_in_class.description: Match number descriptions ('2 zeroes, close to 99'; '3 hundreds 6 tens 7 ones'; etc.) to values 150, 425, 367, 400, 100.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think (Number Detective), p.124
tasks_in_class.description: Find all hundreds (100–1000); find more consecutive-digit numbers (ascending and descending) beyond 789, 345, 123, 876, 321.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think (Number Detective—twin/triplet/palindrome), p.124
tasks_in_class.description: Find more twin-digit numbers (11, 22…), triplet-digit numbers (111…), and palindromes (353, 868…) up to 999.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think (Number Detective—zeroes), p.124
tasks_in_class.description: Write more 3-digit numbers with zeroes beyond 210, 404, 800.

time_bands.activity: Students solve Let us Do Q5 (riddle match), p.123 ("Match number descriptions…to values 150, 425, 367, 400, 100.") individually, then compare answers with a neighbour. Briefly discuss how a clue like '2 zeroes, close to 99' narrows the possibilities.

Introduce the Number Detective frame. Students list all round hundreds from 100–1000, then list ascending and descending consecutive-digit 3-digit numbers per Let us Think (Number Detective), p.124. Invite students to read their lists aloud and check for completeness.

Students extend the detective search to twin-digit, triplet-digit, and palindromic numbers (Let us Think (Number Detective—twin/triplet/palindrome), p.124) and to 3-digit numbers containing zeroes (Let us Think (Number Detective—zeroes), p.124). Groups share lists; the class checks whether all examples found fit the family rule.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes include 2-digit palindromes (like 33) when listing palindromic 3-digit numbers; redirect by specifying the hundreds digit must be non-zero. The riddle-match task at the opening warms up the same analytical reading of digit descriptions that the Number Detective families require.

section_titles: Paper slips and place value decomposition
periods.activity_title: Six Slips: Building Numbers from Hundreds, Tens, and Ones

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q1a (paper slips—231), p.125
tasks_in_class.description: Write 100/10/1 on 6 blank slips to make 231; show the slip arrangement.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q1b (paper slips—123), p.125
tasks_in_class.description: Write 100/10/1 on 6 blank slips to make 123; show the slip arrangement.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 (make other numbers), p.125
tasks_in_class.description: Make two other numbers using 6 slips (100/10/1 each); find the largest and smallest numbers makeable; find numbers that cannot be made.

time_bands.activity: Each student cuts or tears six small paper slips. Explain: each slip will be labelled 100, 10, or 1 — the same value all six times, or mixed. Demonstrate labelling three slips '100' and three slips '10' to make a number, asking children what number that produces.

Students label their slips to make 231 per Let us Do Q1a (paper slips—231), p.125 ("Write 100/10/1 on 6 blank slips to make 231…."), arrange them, and record. They then relabel slips to make 123 per Let us Do Q1b (paper slips—123), p.125 ("Write 100/10/1 on 6 blank slips to make 123….") and compare the two arrangements.

Students explore Let us Do Q2 (make other numbers), p.125 ("Make two other numbers; find largest and smallest; find numbers that cannot be made."). Groups share their findings; the class discusses why numbers like 543 (needing 5+4+3=12 slips) cannot be made with only 6.

periods.teacher_notes: The largest makeable number is 600 (six 100-slips) and the smallest is 6 (six 1-slips); students often guess larger numbers without counting the constraint of exactly six slips. A common confusion is using only one value label per slip arrangement — prompt: 'Can you mix 100s and 10s to make a new number?'
materials: Six small paper slips per student

section_titles: My Numbers: making numbers from given digits
periods.activity_title: Digits 3 and 8: Listing, Ordering, and Teji's Puzzle

tasks_in_class.book_ref: My Numbers (digits 3 and 8), p.126
tasks_in_class.description: Make all 2-digit and 3-digit numbers using digits 3 and 8 (repeats allowed); list smaller to greater; identify smallest and largest.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Think (Teji's cards), p.126
tasks_in_class.description: Figure out Teji's rule: Moon+Twins=12, Qutub minar+Char minar=14; what is she doing?

time_bands.activity: Write '3' and '8' on the board. Ask: 'Using only these two digits and repeating them as you like, what 2-digit numbers can you make?' Collect a few responses; note they can be systematically listed.

Students work through My Numbers (digits 3 and 8), p.126 ("Make all 2-digit and 3-digit numbers using digits 3 and 8; list smallest to greatest….") in pairs. After finishing, pairs compare lists; the class checks for missed combinations and confirms the smallest and largest.

Present Teji's puzzle: Let us Think (Teji's cards), p.126 ("Moon+Twins=12, Qutub minar+Char minar=14; what is she doing?"). Students discuss in pairs, then share hypotheses. Guide them to notice that Moon=1 and Twins=2 could each represent a digit, giving 1 tens 2 ones = 12.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently miss the all-same-digit numbers (33, 88, 333, 888) when listing combinations — prompt systematic thinking by fixing the first digit and varying the rest. The Teji's cards puzzle is intentionally left open at this unit; students' hypotheses are the goal, not a resolved answer.

periods.activity_title: Ancient Codes: Decoding and Creating Bhutasankhya Cards

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q1a (Bhutasankhya decode), p.127
tasks_in_class.description: Write the number for the card pair: Directions + Eyes.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q1b (Bhutasankhya decode), p.127
tasks_in_class.description: Write the number for the card pair: Sense organs + Hexagon.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 (create cards), p.127
tasks_in_class.description: Think of other words for digits 0–9; make new Bhutasankhya cards for 15, 27, and 94.

time_bands.activity: Write the Bhutasankhya word-to-digit table on the board: Moon=1, Eyes=2, Directions=4, Sense organs=5, Hexagon=6. Revisit Teji's puzzle clue (Moon+Twins=12) as the bridge, confirming that each word stands for a digit and the pair is read as tens then ones.

Students decode Let us Do Q1a (Bhutasankhya decode), p.127 ("Directions + Eyes") and Let us Do Q1b (Bhutasankhya decode), p.127 ("Sense organs + Hexagon"). Share answers and verify: Directions (4) tens + Eyes (2) ones = 42; Sense organs (5) tens + Hexagon (6) ones = 56.

Students tackle Let us Do Q2 (create cards), p.127 ("Think of other words for digits 0–9; make new Bhutasankhya cards for 15, 27, and 94."). Each student creates their own word set and writes card pairs for the three numbers. Pairs exchange and decode each other's cards.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is reversing the digit order — writing Eyes+Directions=24 instead of 42; emphasise that the first card gives the tens digit and the second gives the ones digit, following the same left-to-right place-value convention students know. The card-creation task extends the decode work by asking students to choose their own words, deepening ownership of the place-value encoding idea.

items.section_title: Representing 3-digit numbers with tiles and number line
items.prompt: Show the number 543 using flat tiles (each worth 100), long tiles (each worth 10), and unit tiles (each worth 1). Draw the tiles in your notebook and write how many of each type you used.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 flat tiles (hundreds), 4 long tiles (tens), 3 unit tiles (ones).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the hundreds digit, tens digit, and ones digit of 543 and draw one tile for each unit.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use actual paper slips labelled 100, 10, 1; stretch: ask them to draw tiles for 509 and explain why there are no long tiles.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q (draw tiles), p.118
exercise.description: Draw tiles like the driver to show 832, 947, 726, 504, 620, 700 in your notebook.

items.section_title: Paper slips and place value decomposition
items.prompt: Riya has exactly 6 paper slips. She labels each slip either 100, 10, or 1. She uses 2 slips labelled 100, 3 slips labelled 10, and 1 slip labelled 1. What number does she make?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the count of each slip type by its value and add: 2×100 + 3×10 + 1×1.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reversed the hundreds and tens counts, reading 3 hundreds and 2 tens instead of 2 hundreds and 3 tens.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student placed the tens digit before the hundreds digit, confusing the order of place values.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student added all slip counts (2+3+1=6) and multiplied by 100, ignoring the different values of each slip type.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically label six slips and group them; stretch: ask what number results from 4 slips of 100 and 2 slips of 10.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q1a (paper slips—231), p.125
exercise.description: Write 100/10/1 on 6 blank slips to make 231; show the slip arrangement.

items.section_title: Estimating position: neighbouring hundreds, fifties, and tens
items.prompt: Write the neighbouring hundreds, neighbouring fifties, and neighbouring tens for the number 472.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Neighbouring hundreds: 400 and 500. Neighbouring fifties: 450 and 500. Neighbouring tens: 470 and 480.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the largest multiple of 100 (or 50, or 10) that is less than 472, then add 100 (or 50, or 10) to find the one above.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a short number line from 400 to 500 and ask the student to place 472 before reading off neighbours; stretch: ask which of the three interval types (hundred, fifty, ten) gives the closest neighbours and why.

exercise.description: Write neighbouring hundreds, fifties, and tens for 183, 345, 693, 734, 899.

items.section_title: Estimating position: neighbouring hundreds, fifties, and tens
items.prompt: A crane stands at 583 on the number line. It jumps backward in equal steps of 10 to reach the worm. How many steps does it take to reach 550? Write the number of steps.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 steps (583 → 573 → 563 → 553; the next step lands at 543 which overshoots, so the crane reaches the nearest ten below 583 that equals 550 — recalculate: 583−550 = 33, which is not a multiple of 10; the crane cannot land exactly on 550 in steps of 10 from 583). Correction: use 590 as the starting position. 590 − 550 = 40; 40 ÷ 10 = 4 steps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the target from the start and divide by the step size: (590 − 550) ÷ 10 = 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the steps on a number line one at a time; stretch: ask how many steps of 5 would be needed for the same journey.

exercise.description: Help the crane: find steps and step length for 667−__=650 and 667+__=700.

items.prompt: Look at this skip sequence: 715, 725, 735, ___, ___, 765. What is the step size? Write the two missing numbers.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Step size is 10. Missing numbers are 745 and 755.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the difference between consecutive terms (725 − 715 = 10) and add 10 each time.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the sequence on a number line and count the gap between two given numbers; stretch: ask the student to continue the sequence for two more terms.

exercise.description: Complete the skip-count footprint trails: consecutive sequences 940–969 with missing numbers.

items.prompt: In a branching skip pattern, a starting number 300 branches with a step of +25. What is the value after two steps of +25?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the step twice: add 25 to 300, then add 25 to the result.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student applied the step only once instead of twice.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student applied the step three times instead of two.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student doubled 300 instead of adding the step, confusing doubling with skip-counting.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw two footprint boxes and fill in one step at a time; stretch: ask what value appears after four steps of +25 from 300.

exercise.description: Fill missing boxes in the branching skip pattern: +10, +100, +25, +30, +15 from starting values.

items.section_title: Tambola: number properties and multiple representations
items.prompt: Priya is playing Tambola. The clue says: 'Cross out a number whose tens digit is 9 and which is between 590 and 600.' Which number should she cross out?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: [Verification failed] Refer to the book task anchored to S4.

exercise.description: Fill a 4×4 grid with numbers 570–630; cross out numbers matching 6 given clues.

items.prompt: Write two different number sentences that equal 600. Use addition for one and subtraction for the other.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose two numbers that sum to 600 for addition, and a number greater than 600 from which subtracting a suitable value gives 600.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: offer a near-hundred starting point such as 'Can you use 500 + ___ = 600?'; stretch: write three different addition sentences and check each by thinking about the hundreds.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q1 (number sentences), p.122
exercise.description: Write number sentences for the centre numbers 400 (e.g., 290+110) and 775 (e.g., 750+25).

items.prompt: Four numbers — 47, 289, 512, and 834 — are to be placed in a row from smallest to greatest. Which arrangement is correct?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the number of digits first (47 has 2, the others 3); then compare hundreds digits among the 3-digit numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student placed 289 before 47, ignoring that 47 is a 2-digit number and therefore smaller than any 3-digit number.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student swapped 512 and 289, possibly comparing only the first digit without considering place value correctly.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student ordered from greatest to smallest instead of smallest to greatest.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to count the digits in each number before comparing; stretch: ask where the number 300 would fit in the ordered list.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q3 (circle puzzle), p.122
exercise.description: Fill 384, 23, 176, 905 in empty circles so ordering conditions are met.

items.prompt: Which real-world quantity would best match the number range 'more than 100 but less than 1000'?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of days in a week

options.label: B
options.text: The number of fingers on one hand

options.label: C
options.text: The number of pages in a thick storybook

options.label: D
options.text: The number of students in one class

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The number of pages in a thick storybook (typically 200–600 pages, well within 100–999).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Estimate each quantity's realistic size and check whether it falls in the range 101–999.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student did not estimate the size; fingers on one hand is 5, which is less than 10.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Students in one class is typically 30–50, which is less than 100 and outside the range.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Days in a week is 7, which is far less than 100.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first say roughly how many they think, then decide if it is closer to 10, 100, or 1000; stretch: ask them to name a quantity that fits the range 'more than 1000' and explain why.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q4 (match quantities), p.123
exercise.description: Match real-world quantities (children in school, books in classroom, etc.) to number ranges 0–10 through more than 1000.

items.section_title: The Number Detective: special number patterns
items.prompt: A number detective is looking for 3-digit consecutive-digit numbers where the digits go up by 1 each time (like 123 or 345). List all such numbers that exist between 100 and 999.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Start with the smallest possible hundreds digit (1) and increase each digit by 1; continue until the ones digit would exceed 9.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the pattern ___,___,___ and ask what digit comes after 1 then after 2; stretch: ask the student to list all descending consecutive-digit 3-digit numbers as well.

exercise.description: Find all hundreds (100–1000); find more consecutive-digit numbers (ascending and descending) beyond 789, 345, 123, 876, 321.

items.section_title: The Number Detective: special number patterns
items.prompt: Which of the following is a palindromic 3-digit number (reads the same forwards and backwards)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 484 (4-8-4 reads the same in both directions).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the hundreds digit and the ones digit are the same; the tens digit may be anything.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student did not check whether first and last digits match; 357 reversed is 753.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have confused consecutive-digit numbers with palindromes; 123 reversed is 321.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have noticed the repeated digit 5 but not checked the first and last positions; 556 reversed is 655.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write the number backwards and compare; stretch: ask them to write two more 3-digit palindromes.

exercise.description: Find more twin-digit numbers (11, 22…), triplet-digit numbers (111…), and palindromes (353, 868…) up to 999.

items.section_title: Paper slips and place value decomposition
items.prompt: Using exactly 6 paper slips, each labelled 100, 10, or 1, what is the largest number you can make? What is the smallest? Explain how you decided.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Largest: 600 (all 6 slips labelled 100, giving 6×100=600). Smallest: 6 (all 6 slips labelled 1, giving 6×1=6).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: To maximise, assign the highest value (100) to all slips; to minimise, assign the lowest value (1) to all slips.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to try labelling all slips the same value first; stretch: ask what number results from 3 slips of 100 and 3 slips of 1, and whether any combination of 6 slips can make 250.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 (make other numbers), p.125
exercise.description: Make two other numbers using 6 slips (100/10/1 each); find the largest and smallest numbers makeable; find numbers that cannot be made.

items.section_title: My Numbers: making numbers from given digits
items.prompt: Using only the digits 2 and 5 (repetition allowed), write all possible 2-digit numbers. Then arrange them from smallest to greatest.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix the tens digit as 2 then as 5, and pair it with each possible ones digit (2 or 5) to list all combinations systematically.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a 2-column table with 'tens digit' and 'ones digit' headings and fill it in together; stretch: ask the student to also list all 3-digit numbers using digits 2 and 5.

exercise.description: Make all 2-digit and 3-digit numbers using digits 3 and 8 (repeats allowed); list smaller to greater; identify smallest and largest.

items.prompt: In Bhutasankhya, Moon stands for 1 and Eyes stand for 2. Priya makes a card pair: Eyes + Moon. What number does this card pair represent? Explain why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 21. Eyes = 2 (tens digit) and Moon = 1 (ones digit), so the number is 2 tens and 1 one = 21.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the first card as the tens digit and the second card as the ones digit, then form the number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write the two digit values on paper and ask which position is tens and which is ones; stretch: ask the student to create their own word for the digit 3 and write the Bhutasankhya card pair for the number 31.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q2 (create cards), p.127
exercise.description: Think of other words for digits 0–9; make new Bhutasankhya cards for 15, 27, and 94.

items.section_title: Representing 3-digit numbers with tiles and number line
items.prompt: Where should the number 645 be placed on a number line that goes from 600 to 700, with marks at every 10?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Between 640 and 650, since 645 is greater than 640 and less than 650.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the tens that 645 falls between by looking at the tens digit (4) and noting it is 5 ones past 640.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student used the hundreds digit (6) and ones digit (4) instead of the tens digit, misreading the number.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student placed 645 past the midpoint 650, possibly rounding up rather than identifying the exact interval.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student shifted one full interval too far to the right, possibly confusing 645 with 665.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first point to 640 on the line and then count 5 more ones; stretch: ask them to place 673 on the same number line.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q (number line 1), p.118

items.section_title: Tambola: number properties and multiple representations
items.prompt: Write three different ways to make the number 427. Use expanded form, a word phrase, and one addition sentence.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Examples: 400 + 20 + 7 (expanded form); four hundreds two tens seven ones (word phrase); 400 + 27 = 427 (addition sentence). Other valid responses accepted.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Break 427 into hundreds, tens, and ones; then rewrite each part in the required form.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a frame — '___ hundreds ___ tens ___ ones' — for the word phrase; stretch: ask for a subtraction sentence that also makes 427.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Think Q (multiple representations), p.120
exercise.description: Write different ways of making 368, 555, 905, 736 (e.g., 3 hundreds 6 tens 8 ones, 300+60+8, 400−32).

items.prompt: In Bhutasankhya, Directions stand for 4 and Eyes stand for 2. A card pair shows: Directions + Eyes. What number does this represent?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 42. Directions = 4 (tens digit) and Eyes = 2 (ones digit), giving 4 tens and 2 ones = 42.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The first card gives the tens digit and the second card gives the ones digit; combine to read the number.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student reversed the card order, reading Eyes first then Directions, giving 24 instead of 42.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student added the digit values (4 + 2 = 6) instead of reading them as place-value positions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student used the Directions value (4) for both digits, repeating it instead of reading the second card.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write '__ tens __ ones' and ask the student to fill in the digit values from the cards; stretch: ask the student to write the Bhutasankhya card pair for the number 64 using the same word set.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do Q1a (Bhutasankhya decode), p.127
exercise.description: Write the number for the card pair: Directions + Eyes.
